The virtue he found hardest to acquire was **Order** (No. 3).  
Its precept is: *“Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.”*  
Franklin said this scheme “gave me the most trouble” because it was “not possible to be exactly observed by a master, who must mix with the world, and often receive people of business at their own hours.” He noted that even for a journeyman printer it was “extremely difficult to acquire.”

Frederick Douglass first learned to read in Baltimore when his mistress, Mrs. Auld, kindly taught him the alphabet and a few simple words.  
Mr. Auld later forbade further instruction, saying it was “unlawful, as well as unsafe, to teach a slave to read” and that “a nigger should know nothing but to obey his master…learning would spoil the best nigger in the world…if you teach that nigger how to read, there would be no keeping him.”  
Douglass finished learning by befriending white boys in the streets, who taught him, and by carrying a book with him on errands so he could study whenever he had a moment.

Frederick Douglass - self‑taught: learned to read and write with the assistance of his master’s wife.  
Benjamin Franklin - model: Defoe, the first great English journalist and master of the newspaper narrative.  
Frederick Douglass - practice: studied the written language by reading and writing under the guidance of his master’s wife.  
Benjamin Franklin - practice: wrote essays, parables, moral allegories, and apologues in a swift, terse style, emulating Defoe’s journalistic approach.

Benjamin Franklin - apprentice: NOT_FOUND  
Frederick Douglass - sent to Baltimore: 7-8 years old  

Since Franklin’s age at the turning point is not provided, the two ages cannot be directly compared.
